Ask your documents. Then teach a model.

Tejas Patel

16 October 2026

Source: vignettes/articles/introducing-0-4-0.Rmd
introducing-0-4-0.Rmd

dragonfarm 0.4.0 is here, and it hatches from your documents. Feed it PDFs, Word files, and web pages, ask it anything, and it answers in full from what it read. When you want more, it turns the same documents into homework, studies, and fine-tunes a model that knows your material. All from R, on your own machine, free. Raise your own dragon.

Ask it anything

I fed it Costco’s 2024 annual report, all 76 pages, and asked two questions:

Question

Who is Costco’s independent registered public accounting firm?

Costco’s independent registered public accounting firm is KPMG LLP, located in Seattle, WA.

Question

What was net cash used in investing activities in fiscal 2024?

Net cash used in investing activities in fiscal 2024 totaled $4,409 million.

Of thirteen factual questions about the report, it got twelve right. The thirteenth was a figure printed inside a map, and the dragon said the report does not cover it rather than making something up. Good dragon.

Six steps, one app

The app, step by step: drop in documents, ask them with sources, review generated questions, train, watch the loss, compare against the base model.
  1. Documents. Feed it PDFs, Word files, web pages, spreadsheets, or a whole folder.
  2. Ask. Get full answers drawn from your documents.
  3. Teach. It writes its own practice questions and answers from your documents. You keep the good ones.
  4. Train. It studies the pairs you kept.
  5. Monitor. Watch it learn.
  6. Try it. Put the trained dragon next to the wild one, both answering from your documents.

Your documents never leave your machine. No GPU? dragonfarm sends the training to a free Colab or Kaggle GPU and brings the dragon home.

What you get

  • Full answers, in plain words. It reads the relevant parts of your documents and answers the question, not just points you at a page.
  • An honest “not covered”. Ask about something the documents do not contain and it says so.
  • Training data you did not have to write. Most people who want to fine-tune have documents, not a table of questions and answers. The dragon writes the table; you mark it.
  • A model that is yours. It runs on your machine and loads anywhere with standard tools. No subscription, no leash.
  • The right size for your nest. An 8 GB laptop GPU raises a 7B dragon; smaller cards and CPUs get a smaller one, picked for you.

How big a dragon do you need?

The same questions, the same documents, four sizes, one 8 GB laptop GPU, before any training:

Dragon Annual report: right of 23 R manuals: right of 32 Said “not covered” when true, of 20
Hatchling (0.5B) 17 19 16
Drake (1.5B) 19 28 20
Wyvern (3B) 20 30 20
Elder (7B) 23 31 20

And after training:

  • The Elder, trained on R’s manuals, stayed exactly as accurate and picked up manners: shorter, tidier answers.
  • On support tickets, a dragon trained this way recalled 89 percent of the policy facts on tickets it had never seen, against 68 percent for ordinary fine-tuning. When the policy changed after training, it followed the new version in 88 percent of answers. Old dragon, new tricks.
  • For a fixed format such as turning tickets into JSON, even the Hatchling scored 20 of 20 after a few minutes of training.

The details are in Choosing a model size.

Where dragons fear to tread

  • Questions that need every row of a spreadsheet (“which year had the highest margin?”) are better answered in R, on the data.
  • Scanned pages need OCR first, and numbers inside charts are lost.
  • Small dragons trained on a few hundred examples can get cocky. Review the practice questions, and let a bigger dragon do the answering.
  • These numbers come from a handful of documents, not yours. Try it on yours.

Hatch one

dragonfarm reaches CRAN in November. Until then, get it from R-universe, which builds it for Windows, Mac, and Linux. Then open the app with dragon_app(), or follow the quickstart.

dragonfarm is MIT licensed. Issues, documents that break it, and pull requests are welcome at github.com/tejas4patel/dragonfarm, and there are a few good first issues for new dragon keepers.
